summary: TRILL is based on IS-IS, which supports multilevel routing, but extending TRILL to several levels raises new problems, such as distributing multi-destination traffic and handling switch nicknames. This informational document discusses alternatives for solving them.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 8243 looks at how to split a large TRILL network into smaller areas. TRILL switches in different areas exchange traffic through a Level 2 backbone, and the RFC compares two ways of naming those switches: one where every switch has a nickname that is unique across the whole campus, and one where a nickname identifies the area instead. The document recommends design options; it defines no protocol.

subtitle: How a TRILL network can be split into areas, and what that costs at the border between them.

tldr.problem: TRILL uses IS-IS link state routing over a flat campus, so as the network grows the routing computation, the link state database, the convergence time and the number of 16-bit nicknames all become hard limits.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC examines two ways to run TRILL over multiple levels: unique nicknames that are unique across the whole campus, and aggregated nicknames where each area has one nickname that stands for the area and border switches rewrite the nickname fields as packets cross levels.
tldr.outcome: Aggregated nicknames remove the nickname limit but cost complexity in border switches, so the RFC recommends a campus that may contain both kinds of area, starting with unique nicknames and adding aggregated areas as the network grows.

facts.label: Campus that exhausts unique nicknames
facts.value: 200 areas of 500 switches needs 100,000 or more nicknames

today: RFC 8243 is an Informational document published in September 2017 that weighs design alternatives for multilevel TRILL. No RFC obsoletes or updates it, so it remains guidance for anyone extending TRILL rather than a specification to implement.

sections.title: Scaling Limits of a Single-Level TRILL Campus
sections.content:
TRILL, the IETF Transparent Interconnection of Lots of Links protocol, provides optimal pairwise data routing without configuration, safe forwarding even during periods of temporary loops, and multipathing of unicast and multicast traffic. It does this by running the IS-IS link state routing protocol together with a header that carries a hop count. Devices that implement TRILL are called TRILL switches, or RBridges.

The motivation for multilevel TRILL is scalability. The document lists the issues that can limit a TRILL network: the routing computation load; the volatility of the link state database (LSDB) creating too much control traffic; that volatility causing the network to spend too much time unconverged; the size of the LSDB; the limit on the number of TRILL switches imposed by the 16-bit nickname space; the traffic caused by upper-layer use of broadcast and multicast; and the size of the end-node learning table, which remembers (egress TRILL switch, label or Media Access Control address) pairs.

IS-IS was designed to be multilevel. A network can be partitioned into areas; routing within an area is Level 1 routing and routing between areas is Level 2 routing. Level 2 routers may also take part in one or more Level 1 areas. Each area connects to Level 2 through one or more border routers, and care is needed so that exactly one border TRILL switch transitions a particular packet between the levels, otherwise traffic is duplicated or lost.

The document quantifies the benefit. With N switches in a campus and k links per switch, the Dijkstra computation in a single-level campus is on the order of N*k*log(N); in an optimized multilevel campus whose Level 1 areas hold sqrt(N) switches, it is on the order of sqrt(N)*k*log(N). For N of 3,000 that is a reduction by about a factor of 50. The LSDB size and the rate of LSDB change both improve by about a factor of sqrt(N), and the time spent unconverged improves by about a factor of N. The end-node learning table is the one issue multilevel does not help.
sections.plainLanguage: A flat TRILL network makes every switch redo the whole routing calculation and keep the whole map of the network. Splitting the network into areas means each switch only handles its own area, and a Level 2 backbone connects the areas. The document works out that this cuts the routing work by roughly the square root of the network size.

sections.title: Unique and Aggregated Nicknames
sections.content:
RBridges are designated by 16-bit nicknames for many TRILL purposes. Some values are reserved, which still leaves enough nicknames to designate over 65,000 RBridges, but the number is effectively reduced by two factors. Pseudo-nicknames are consumed for the active-active connection of end stations, which could double nickname consumption where extensive active-active edge groups connect to different sets of edge switch ports. And with a single flat pool, switches in different areas contend for the same nicknames, so a hierarchical allocation in which Level 2 hands blocks of nicknames to Level 1 areas is likely, and that wastes nicknames in the same way hierarchical IP address allocation does.

Even without those reductions, a campus with 200 areas of 500 switches would need 100,000 or more nicknames if every nickname had to be unique across the campus, which is impossible with 16 bits. Only the aggregated-nickname approach addresses that limit.

In the unique-nickname alternative, all nicknames across the campus must be unique. Border TRILL switches are simpler because they do not modify the TRILL header, and testing and maintenance of traffic that starts in one area and ends in another is simpler. The cost is that each area needs a block of nicknames, and the border switch has to announce which nicknames are taken. Because nickname information in Type-Length-Value (TLV) items is encoded by listing individual nicknames, telling an area that it holds all the others would mean tens of thousands of individual entries in the Level 1 LSDB. The preferred fix is a new TLV, similar to the Nickname Flags sub-TLV of RFC 7780 but carrying flags for blocks of nicknames rather than single nicknames, which would require a software update.

In the aggregated-nickname alternative, nicknames inside an aggregated-nickname area are only locally significant and the only nickname visible outside is the area nickname, which stands for all the internal nicknames. Border TRILL switches replace either the ingress or the egress nickname field in the TRILL header of unicast packets with the aggregated nickname of the area. This eliminates nickname exhaustion, reduces the amount of nickname information passed between areas, minimizes the size of the forwarding table, and simplifies the RPF (Reverse Path Forwarding) check, since only the area nickname needs to appear rather than all the ingress TRILL switches in that area. An area can be identified either by a 16-bit nickname assigned to the area, which is not the nickname of any actual switch, or by the set of nicknames of its border routers.
sections.plainLanguage: TRILL switches are named by a 16-bit nickname, and there are only so many. The RFC compares two ways to cope. With unique nicknames, every switch in the whole campus has its own nickname, so border switches do nothing special to packets. With aggregated nicknames, each area gets one nickname of its own and the switches inside use nicknames that only mean something locally, so border switches rewrite the nickname fields in the TRILL header as a packet moves between areas.

sections.title: How a Packet Crosses Two Areas
sections.content:
The border learning variation of aggregated nicknames is worked through with an example. RB2 and RB3 are border TRILL switches, a source S is attached to RB1, and the two areas have nicknames 15961 and 15918. RB1 has nickname 27 and RB4 has nickname 44; the text notes that RB1 and RB4 could even have the same nickname, since the switch nickname is not visible outside these aggregated-nickname areas.

When S transmits a frame to destination D, and D's location has already been learned, RB1 encapsulates the frame in a TRILL header with ingress RBridge 27 and egress 15918. RB2 has announced in the Level 1 IS-IS instance of area 15961 that it is attached to all the area nicknames, including 15918, so IS-IS routes the packet to RB2. When transitioning the packet from Level 1 to Level 2, RB2 replaces the ingress TRILL switch nickname with the area nickname, changing 27 to 15961. Within Level 2 the ingress RBridge field is therefore 15961 and the egress RBridge field is 15918. The packet is forwarded through Level 2 to RB3, which has advertised reachability to nickname 15918 in Level 2. When forwarding into area 15918, RB3 replaces the egress nickname with RB4's nickname 44, so inside the destination area the ingress nickname is 15961 and the egress nickname is 44. RB4, on decapsulating, learns that S is attached to nickname 15961.

The nickname fields therefore follow fixed rules. When both the ingress and egress switches are in the same area, nothing changes. Between Level 1 areas in Level 2, the ingress nickname is the nickname of the ingress switch's area and the egress nickname is a nickname of the egress switch's area or a tree nickname. Going from Level 1 to Level 2, the ingress nickname is the ingress switch's own nickname. Coming from Level 2 to Level 1, the ingress nickname is a nickname for the ingress switch's area and the egress nickname is the egress switch's own nickname or a tree nickname.

Two variations of the aggregated approach are compared. Border learning, described above, minimizes the change in non-border switches but puts the burden on border switches to learn and look up the end-station MAC addresses in their area that are used for communication outside the area; the burden can be reduced by making areas smaller and more numerous. The swap nickname field variant adds an ingress swap nickname field and an egress swap nickname field to TRILL Data packets, so RB2 moves the ingress nickname into the ingress swap field and inserts the area nickname, and RB3 swaps the egress nickname and egress swap fields. That removes the extra address learning burden from border switches but requires changes to the TRILL Data packet header and more extensive changes to non-border switches, which must associate both a switch nickname and an area nickname with end-station MAC and label pairs. The document concludes that the changes to the TRILL header and fast-path processing make the swap variant impractical for the foreseeable future.
sections.plainLanguage: Here is the mechanism in the RFC's own example. A host sends a frame, and its local switch wraps it in a TRILL header naming the switch that received it and the area the destination is in. The border switch in the sending area swaps the receiving switch's nickname for the area's nickname before passing the packet into the Level 2 backbone. The border switch in the receiving area then swaps the area nickname for the nickname of the switch the destination is plugged into.

sections.title: Area Addresses and Area Nicknames
sections.content:
Each area is configured with an area address, advertised in IS-IS messages so that areas are not accidentally interconnected. For TRILL the only purpose of the area address is to avoid accidentally merging areas, although the area address had other purposes in CLNP (ConnectionLess Network Protocol), for which IS-IS was originally designed. The TRILL base specification says the area address must be zero; zero was also chosen as a safety mechanism so that Layer 3 IS-IS packets would not be confused with TRILL IS-IS packets, although TRILL uses other techniques such as different multicast addresses and Ethertypes on Ethernet to avoid that confusion.

Current TRILL switches reject any IS-IS message with a non-zero area address, so the document lists four choices: upgrade all switches that will interoperate in a multilevel environment to understand non-zero area addresses; have neighbours of old switches remove the area address from IS-IS messages when talking to them, which might break IS-IS security or cause inadvertent merging of areas; ignore the risk of accidental merging; or keep the fixed area address field at zero and add a new optional TLV for an area name to Hellos, which new switches could compare to prevent accidental merging. A simple solution to the first choice is for each switch to use a dominant area nickname as its area address: for the unique-nickname alternative the lowest value nickname held by any border RBridge of the area, and for the aggregated-nickname alternative the lowest nickname held by a border RBridge or a nickname representing the area.

In the aggregated-nickname alternative, each area must acquire a unique identifier, for example by acquiring a unique area nickname or by using an identifier based on the area's set of border TRILL switches. It is probably simpler to allocate a block of nicknames, for example the top 4000, to represent areas rather than specific TRILL switches. The nicknames used for area identification are advertised and acquired through Level 2. Within an area, border TRILL switches find each other through the Level 1 LSDB, either by using the IS-IS attached bit or by explicitly advertising in their LSP that they are a border RBridge. One of them, with the highest priority, can take part in Level 2 to acquire a nickname for the area, or can give the area a pseudonode IS-IS ID such as RB7.5 within Level 2, so that the area appears in Level 2 as a pseudonode that acquires the nickname.

The election of the Designated Border RBridge (DBRB) within an area is done through LSPs within the area, because border TRILL switches are not necessarily physical neighbours of each other. The DBRB acquires the area nickname, may give the area a pseudonode IS-IS ID, and advertises both in the area. The Level 1 LSPs it originates for the area carry information external to the area, such as nicknames of external areas and pruning information such as multicast listeners and labels. All the other border TRILL switches announce attachment to the area. Within Level 2 the DBRB generates a Level 2 LSP on behalf of the area, and all of the area's border TRILL switches announce connection to the area in their Level 2 LSPs.
sections.plainLanguage: Each area needs a name of its own so that two areas are not joined by accident. The RFC compares four ways to get one, and settles on the simplest: every switch in an area uses the same area address, taken from the lowest nickname among the area's border switches. The area's border switches then elect one of themselves to speak for the area to the Level 2 backbone.

sections.title: Multi-Destination Trees, RPF and Scope
sections.content:
Multi-destination packets are distributed along trees rooted at TRILL switches. It is easy to build a multi-area tree by building a tree in each area separately, including the Level 2 area, and having a single border TRILL switch in each area attach to Level 2, but that removes the desire to split paths so that not all multi-destination traffic goes through the same border switch. That is the same problem as multiple ingress switches injecting traffic from a pseudonode, and it can be solved with the affinity TLV of RFC 7783, where for each tree in the area at most one border RBridge announces itself with that tree name.

The RPF check for trees works differently depending on where the packet came from. For multi-destination data originating inside an area, the check is computed as today. For packets originating outside the area, the check must be based on which of the border TRILL switches injected the packet into the area, so a switch inside the area has to know which border switch made the transition. This could be done by having the DBRB announce the transitioner assignments to all TRILL switches in the area, by using the affinity sub-TLV mechanism of RFC 7783, or with a new tree encoding.

Marking a multi-destination packet with a scope that says it should not exit the area is desirable for two reasons: to address the case where a unicast packet becomes multi-destination on the way from Level 2 to Level 1, and to constrain the broadcast domain for discovery, directory or service protocols. The technique that might require the least change to TRILL switch fast-path logic would be to indicate the scope in the egress nickname that designates the distribution tree, for example with two tree nicknames per tree, one for area-restricted and one for multi-area distribution, or with a set of special currently reserved nicknames. A packet that is converted from unicast to multi-destination on arrival at a border switch must be restricted to the destination area, otherwise the designated transitioner may pick it up and flood it back into Level 2, where it can be flooded into multiple areas. Alternatively, the packet could be tunnelled within the area to the appointed transitioner with instructions to transmit it only inside the area.

A new tree encoding is described for completeness: instead of using all 16 bits of the egress nickname field for the nickname of the tree root, TRILL could use the bottom 6 bits for the tree number, allowing 64 trees, and leave 10 bits for a scope flag and an indicator of which of the border switches injected the packet. This would require all TRILL switches to change, so its deployment is not practical at the time of writing.

Selective broadcast domain reduction covers service and discovery protocols such as DHCP, the NetBIOS Service Location Protocol and multicast DNS, which are reached through multicast or broadcast frames. Such protocols often restrict distribution to an IP subnet and provide a proxy that reaches the service elsewhere by unicast. With multilevel TRILL, very large IP subnets could become saturated with this kind of multi-destination traffic unless packets can be restricted further. One way is to keep protocol P traffic inside the area, or to stop border switches transitioning it, and to place a protocol P proxy in each area that unicasts requests to the campus servers and delivers the replies inside the area.
sections.plainLanguage: Broadcast and multicast traffic follows trees of switches. When the tree crosses areas, the switches inside an area need to know which border switch the packet came in through, so they can check that the packet arrived on the expected path. The RFC also explains why a packet that turns from a single destination into a broadcast part way must be marked to stay inside its area.

sections.title: Coexistence with Old TRILL Switches
sections.content:
TRILL switches that are not multilevel aware may have trouble calculating the RPF check and filtering information, because they do not know which border switch does the transition. A possible solution, as long as old switches exist within an area, is for the border switches to elect a single DBRB and route all inter-area traffic through it, unicast as well as multi-destination. If that DBRB goes down, a new one is elected. The cost is that load splitting at the level transition is eliminated.

Multi-access links with end stations need care. End stations know nothing about TRILL, so it is essential that only one TRILL switch ingresses or egresses any given packet to or from an end station, so that connectivity is provided without duplicating data and without loops forming when one switch egresses data in native form, with no TRILL header, and another switch on the link re-ingresses it. In single-level TRILL this is done by electing a single Designated RBridge per link, which appoints a single Appointed Forwarder per VLAN, a mechanism that depends on the RBridges establishing adjacency.

The problem arises when two TRILL switches on the same link are in different areas. If they ignore each other's Hellos, as normal IS-IS PDU processing rules require for different areas, they will not form an adjacency, and the Appointed Forwarder mechanism will not pick one of them, so both will ingress and egress end-station traffic on the link, causing loops and duplication. The preferred simple rule is to use the TRILL switch or switches with the lowest-numbered area, comparing area numbers as unsigned integers, to handle all native traffic to and from end stations on the link. That automatically gives multilevel-ignorant legacy switches, which use area number zero, the highest priority. A multilevel-aware switch that sees Hellos from lower-numbered areas would not act as an Appointed Forwarder on the link until the Hello timer for those Hellos had expired.

The document also notes that an area may become partitioned so that a path between two sections exists only via the Level 2 area, in which case multilevel TRILL will naturally break the area into two areas. If the Level 2 area is partitioned in a way that could be healed by a path through a Level 1 area, TRILL will not attempt to solve it: multi-destination data reaches only the portion of the campus reachable through the partition attached to the transition switch, but no loop forms.
sections.plainLanguage: Older TRILL switches do not understand areas. As long as any of them are present, the document suggests routing all traffic between areas through one elected border switch, which is simpler but removes the ability to spread that traffic over several borders. It also gives a rule for a shared link where switches in different areas meet: the switch in the lowest-numbered area handles the ordinary traffic of the attached devices.
